```{r in-a-nutshell, echo = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
## Packages
library("devtools")
my_pkg <- "mypkg"
setwd(paste0("~/.R-site/packages/", my_pkg))

## README.Rmd → README.md
devtools::build_readme()

## Load, document and check
load_all()
document()
run_examples()
check()

## Install
install()

## CRAN
check_win_oldrelease()
check_win_release()
check_win_devel()
submit_cran()

## Reset GitHub credentials
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
credentials::set_github_pat()
```

This document briefly explains the minimal steps to write a package for
R. Detailed information are given in the ["R Packages" online
book](https://r-pkgs.org/) by Hadley Wickham and Jennifer Bryan and the R manual
["Writing R
Extensions"](http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html). This tutorial
makes extensive use of the [package
`devtools`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=devtools), but also relies on the
base R package `tools`, as well as packages `roxygen2`, `testthat`, and `knitr`,
and eventually `pkgdown` and `nanonext` to create a companion website. Let's
install them now:

```{r pkg-install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "testthat", "knitr", "pkgdown", "nanonext"))
```

We load at least `devtools`, which provides most relevant functions (and also
attach package `usethis` for other important ones):

```{r pkg, eval = FALSE}
library("devtools")
```

## Package structure

We start by setting the name of the package and creating it (I have my packages
in `~/.R-site/packages/`):

```{r create, eval = FALSE}
my_pkg <- "mypkg"
create_package(paste0("~/.R-site/packages/", my_pkg))
```

This create the most minimal package structure, with the following structure:

    <mypkg>/
    +-- R/
    +-- DESCRIPTION
    +-- NAMESPACE

* `R/`: A folder which contains all R source code;
* `DESCRIPTION`: A file which provides metadata about the package;
* `NAMESPACE`: A file which describes the functions available for others to
  use. It will be automatically generated.

We then need to edit the content of the `DESCRIPTION` file (which comes with a
template already). An example would look like the following (note it will be
reformatted in the process, such as line breaks):

```
Package: basr
Title: Basic, but Hopefully Useful, Functions
Version: 1.1.0
Date: 2026-11-12
Authors@R: c(
    person("Mathieu", "Basille", email = "mathieu@basille.org",
        role = c("aut", "cre", "cph"),
        comment = c(ORCID = "0000-0001-9366-7127")))
Description: Collection of basic functions for a variety of usage (data,
    statistics, graphs, package management, utils), mostly for my own
    convenience.
URL: https://github.com/basille/basr
Suggests:
    devtools,
    httpgd,
    knitr,
    pak,
    sessioninfo
License: MIT + file LICENSE
Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1
Encoding: UTF-8
Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
```

**Note:** If the package is already created, we simply name it and set the
working directory to the proper folder:

```{r wd, eval = FALSE}
my_pkg <- "mypkg"
setwd(paste0("~/.R-site/packages/", my_pkg))
```

A good place to describe the package is in the file `README.Rmd`, which can be
properly initialised with:

```{r readme-init, eval = FALSE}
usethis::use_readme_rmd()
```

The following command produces `README.md`, which is used in the GitHub
repository for instance:


```{r readme-build, eval = FALSE}
devtools::build_readme()
```

## R code and documentation

The R source code can then be placed in the `R` directory, preferably with one
file per function (or group of functions) or a single R file with all the code
`/R/mypkg-package.R`. All functions and data sets, as well as the package
itself, must be documented following the `roxygen2` syntax directly in the
source code (see [details here](https://r-pkgs.org/man.html)). When the
functions are ready to use, they can be loaded (with a result similar to a call
to `library("<mypkg>")` for a regularly installed package) via:

```{r load, eval = FALSE}
load_all()
```

If the `roxygen2` tags are properly completed in the R source code, we can
proceed to update the documentation (`.Rd` files, `DESCRIPTION` and
`NAMESPACE`):

```{r doc, eval = FALSE}
document()
```

The documentation itself is generated in a new folder, which contains help files
(`.Rd`) for each documented function (or group of functions):

    <mypkg>/
    +-- man
    |   +-- <files>.Rd
    +-- R
    |   +-- <files>.R
    +-- DESCRIPTION
    +-- NAMESPACE

## Check and test

A series of checks can then be run, first on the examples, and then more
generally on the package structure and content:

```{r check, eval = FALSE}
run_examples()
check()
```

If problems such as "Error : extractFromURL.Rd: non-ASCII input and no declared
encoding" arrise, we can use the `tools` package to identify which is (are) the
faulty line(s):

```{r asci, eval = FALSE}
tools::showNonASCII(readLines("/man/XXX.Rd"))
```

For complex packages, it might be useful to prepare and run a battery of
[tests](https://r-pkgs.org/testing-basics.html).

```{r test, eval = FALSE}
test()
```

Now don't forget to write the changelog and news in the NEWS file, as well as
updating other documentation files (see
[details](https://r-pkgs.org/other-markdown.html)). If necessary, update the
`README.md` file as well (with `devtools::build_readme()`).

If required, the PDF manual can be easily generated with the function `manual`
from `basr`, which is wrapper to `R CMD Rd2pdf`. The function needs the package
name or path as input. Options include the target directory (by default, the
package directory, which is where I leave them), and two additional options to
preview (`preview = TRUE` by default) or overwrite (`overwrite = FALSE` by
default) the PDF.

```{r manual, eval = FALSE}
basr::manual()
basr::manual(overwrite = TRUE)
## manual(path = "src/contrib", preview = FALSE, overwrite = TRUE)

## Check argument 'manual' in 'build' (FALSE by default)
```

## Installation and packaging

The package is now ready to install. The package can be directly installed
locally:

```{r install-local, eval = FALSE}
install()
install(build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

To distribute the package, the easiest way is to publish it in a GitHub
repository. The package can then simply be installed with the help of the
package [`remotes`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=remotes) or, better,
[`pak`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pak):


```{r install-remote, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("<repo>/<pkg>")
pak::pkg_install("<repo>/<pkg>")
```

To reach a wider audience, and allow better inclusion in the R package
ecosystem, it is interesting to consider a submission to CRAN (expect
difficulties). [Follow the checklist](https://r-pkgs.org/release.html) step by
step to ensure a successful submission.

Note that there is a special web service called
[Win-builder](http://win-builder.r-project.org/) that checks packages against
Windows systems. This service uses the e-mail address specified in the
"Maintainer" field of the package's `DESCRIPTION` file to send the result of the
process. We can check packages against the previous major release version of R,
the current release and the development version (the last two need at least to
be checked):

```{r build-win, eval = FALSE}
check_win_oldrelease()
check_win_release()
check_win_devel()
```

If all checks are successful and all files are properly updated and documented
(including comments for CRAN in `cran-comments.md`), the package can be released
to CRAN:

```{r cran, eval = FALSE}
submit_cran()
```

## Companion website

With the help of a the package `pkgdown`, it is super easy to create a nice,
user-friendly website, that can be hosted for instance on GitHub Pages. You
first need to create (or check) a temporary [Personal access
tokens](https://github.com/settings/tokens/) (PAT) to GitHub with:

```{r gitcreds, eval = FALSE}
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
credentials::set_github_pat()
```

Then let `pkgdown` initialise the configuration with the following command (to
run only once):

```{r web-init-ghpages, eval = FALSE}
usethis::use_pkgdown_github_pages()
```

What it does:

- Creates `_pkgdown.yml`, which is the main configuration file for pkgdown.
- Adds various patterns to `.Rbuildignore`, to keep pkgdown-specific files and
  directories from being included in your package bundle.
- Adds `docs`, the default destination for a rendered site, to `.gitignore`.
- Creates a dedicated branch `gh-pages` for the website.
- Initiate GitHub Pages on the repository and configures it.
- Use the GitHub Pages URL as the home page of the package (including in
  `DESCRIPTION`).

Note that you need to add the `.github/` folder to the tracked files, and push
it to GitHub.

Then to render the website locally, use:

```{r web-local, eval = FALSE}
pkgdown::build_site()
```

To have a nice organisation of the functions, edit `_pkgdown.yml` and add
something like this, with as many subsections as needed (see details in
[pkgdown::build_reference](https://pkgdown.r-lib.org/reference/build_reference.html)):


```
reference:
- title: Basic, but Hopefully Useful, Functions
- subtitle: Data management
  desc: |
    Functions to handle data from vectors and data frames.
  contents:
  - colNAs
  - extrange
  - kcut
  - …
```

Now every time a commit is pushed on the GitHub repository, GitHub Actions will
build the website and make it available at `https://<user>.github.io/<mypkg/`
(it will take a few minutes for the magic to work remotely). 

<!-- If you get a **404 error**, be sure to check that the GitHub Pages link to the -->
<!-- `/docs` folder of the `gh-pages` branch (under Settings > Pages > Build and -->
<!-- deployment). -->
